sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 14.3 DNA Replication in Eukaryotes

terms.definition: DNA copying in which each daughter double helix contains one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand.
A DNA sequence where replication proteins assemble and DNA synthesis begins.
A Y-shaped region where parental DNA strands separate and new strands are synthesized.
An enzyme that uses ATP to unwind a DNA double helix at a replication fork.
An enzyme that relieves torsional strain ahead of a replication fork by cutting and rejoining DNA.
A protein that stabilizes separated DNA strands and prevents them from re-pairing during replication.
A short RNA segment providing a free 3′ hydroxyl group for DNA polymerase.
An RNA polymerase that synthesizes primers needed to begin DNA replication.
An enzyme that extends DNA from a primer by adding complementary nucleotides to a 3′ end.
The daughter strand synthesized continuously toward the advancing replication fork.
The daughter strand synthesized discontinuously away from the replication fork as short fragments.
A short DNA segment produced during discontinuous synthesis of the lagging strand.
An enzyme that seals breaks in a sugar–phosphate backbone by forming phosphodiester bonds.
Detection and removal of an incorrectly paired nucleotide during or immediately after DNA synthesis.
A repetitive DNA–protein structure that protects the end of a linear chromosome.
An RNA-containing enzyme that extends chromosome ends using its internal RNA as a template.
A DNA sequence that contributes to a functional RNA or polypeptide product.
Synthesis of an RNA strand complementary to a DNA template.
An enzyme that synthesizes RNA in the 5′-to-3′ direction from a DNA template.
A DNA region where transcription machinery binds to initiate RNA synthesis.
A sequence or structural signal that causes transcription to stop and the RNA transcript to be released.
A newly transcribed eukaryotic messenger RNA precursor that still requires processing.
Modification of a primary RNA transcript, including capping, polyadenylation, and splicing in eukaryotes.
A transcribed sequence removed from a precursor RNA during splicing.
A sequence retained in a mature RNA after splicing.
A complex of small nuclear RNAs and proteins that removes introns from pre-mRNA.
A processed messenger RNA ready to be exported and translated in a eukaryotic cell.
A three-nucleotide sequence in mRNA that specifies an amino acid or translation stop.
The rules relating mRNA codons to amino acids and translation signals.
Synthesis of a polypeptide as a ribosome reads the codon sequence of mRNA.
An adaptor RNA that carries a specific amino acid and base-pairs with an mRNA codon.
A three-nucleotide tRNA sequence that base-pairs antiparallel with a complementary mRNA codon.
An enzyme that attaches the correct amino acid to its corresponding tRNA.
The mRNA triplet AUG that establishes the reading frame and usually encodes methionine.
An mRNA triplet that recruits a release factor instead of an aminoacyl-tRNA, ending translation.
Multiple ribosomes simultaneously translating the same mRNA molecule.

sourceTitle: NHGRI Genetics Glossary and Genome Editing

terms.definition: A heritable change in the nucleotide sequence of genetic material.
A sequence change affecting a single nucleotide position.
Replacement of one nucleotide pair by a different nucleotide pair.
Addition of one or more nucleotides to a DNA sequence.
Removal of one or more nucleotides from a DNA sequence.
An insertion or deletion not divisible by three that changes the downstream coding frame.
A coding-sequence change that does not alter the encoded amino acid.
A coding-sequence change that replaces one amino acid with another in a polypeptide.
A coding-sequence change that converts an amino-acid codon into a premature stop codon.
A physical, chemical, or biological agent that increases mutation frequency.
A sequence change in a non-germline cell that is passed to daughter cells but not normally to offspring.
A sequence change in a gamete-forming lineage that can be inherited by offspring.
A genome-editing system in which guide RNA directs a Cas9 nuclease to a chosen DNA target.
An engineered RNA that base-pairs with target DNA and positions a CRISPR-associated nuclease.
An RNA-guided enzyme that cuts both strands of target DNA near a suitable PAM sequence.
A short DNA motif adjacent to a target that is required for binding and cutting by a CRISPR nuclease.
Deliberate disruption or removal of a gene to prevent production of its functional product.
An unintended genome change at a sequence resembling the intended editing target.
The ordered sequence of cell growth, DNA replication, nuclear division, and cell division.
The cell-cycle period comprising G1, S, and G2, when a cell grows and duplicates its DNA.
The first gap phase, when a cell grows and carries out normal functions before DNA synthesis.
The interphase stage during which nuclear DNA is replicated.
The second gap phase, when a cell prepares for nuclear division after DNA replication.
Division of a eukaryotic nucleus that ordinarily produces genetically equivalent daughter nuclei.
The mitotic stage when chromosomes condense and the spindle begins to form.
The mitotic stage when duplicated chromosomes align at the spindle equator.
The mitotic stage when sister chromatids separate and move toward opposite poles.
The mitotic stage when chromosomes arrive at poles, decondense, and new nuclear envelopes form.
Physical division of a cell’s cytoplasm into separate daughter cells.
One continuous DNA molecule with associated proteins, carrying part of a cell’s genetic information.
One of two replicated chromosome copies joined before their separation during division.
A chromosome region that holds sister chromatids together and supports kinetochore assembly.
A protein structure assembled at a centromere where spindle microtubules attach.
A microtubule-based apparatus that organizes and separates chromosomes during nuclear division.
Two nuclear divisions after one DNA replication that usually produce four genetically varied haploid cells.
A maternal and paternal chromosome pair carrying the same genes at corresponding loci.
Pairing of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis.
Reciprocal DNA exchange between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during meiosis I.
Random orientation of homologous pairs at meiosis I, generating different maternal and paternal chromosome combinations.
Having one complete set of chromosomes.
Having two homologous sets of chromosomes.
Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate correctly during cell division.
Use of genetic information to produce a functional RNA or polypeptide.
A regulatory protein that binds DNA and influences transcription initiation.
A regulatory DNA sequence that increases transcription when bound by activating proteins.
A regulatory DNA sequence that reduces transcription when bound by repressing proteins.
Study of heritable or persistent changes in gene activity that do not alter DNA sequence.
Covalent addition of methyl groups to DNA, often associated with reduced transcription in eukaryotes.
Covalent alteration of histone tails that changes chromatin accessibility or recruits regulatory proteins.
The DNA–protein complex that packages eukaryotic chromosomes.
Relatively open chromatin that is generally accessible to transcription machinery.
Densely packed chromatin that is generally less transcriptionally active.
A chromatin unit consisting of DNA wrapped around a core of histone proteins.
A prokaryotic regulatory unit in which one promoter controls transcription of multiple genes.
An inducible bacterial gene cluster that regulates lactose uptake and metabolism.
A regulatory protein that reduces gene transcription by binding a specific DNA site or transcription factor.
A small molecule that increases gene expression by altering a regulatory protein’s activity.
Production of different mature RNAs from one precursor by selecting different exon combinations.
Sequence-specific reduction of gene expression directed by small RNA molecules.
A short regulatory RNA that pairs with target mRNA to reduce translation or promote degradation.

sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 30.5 Transport of Water and Solutes in Plants

terms.definition: The potential energy of water relative to pure water that predicts movement from higher to lower values.
The non-positive contribution of dissolved solutes to water potential; adding solute makes it more negative.
The contribution of physical pressure to water potential, positive under compression and negative under tension.
Net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from higher to lower water potential.
A solution with higher effective solute concentration than the reference, causing susceptible cells to lose water.
A solution with lower effective solute concentration than the reference, causing susceptible cells to gain water.
A solution producing no net water movement across a membrane relative to the reference cell or solution.
Separation of a plant cell’s plasma membrane from its wall after water loss in a hypertonic solution.
Outward pressure of a plant cell’s contents against its wall after water entry.
A plant cell firm from water uptake and high positive pressure against its wall.
A plant cell with insufficient internal pressure to remain firm.
A membrane channel protein that selectively increases water permeability.
The total concentration of osmotically active particles per liter of solution.
A difference in water potential that drives net water movement from a higher value to a lower value.
The condition at which a plant cell’s plasma membrane is just beginning to pull away from the wall.

sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 43 Animal Reproduction and Development

terms.definition: Production of offspring from one parent without fusion of gametes.
Production of offspring involving meiosis and fusion of haploid gametes.
A haploid reproductive cell capable of fusing with another during fertilization.
Fusion of haploid gamete nuclei to form a diploid zygote.
The diploid cell formed by fusion of two haploid gametes.
A reproductive organ that produces gametes and sex hormones.
Production and maturation of sperm from diploid germ cells in the testes.
Production and maturation of female gametes from diploid germ cells in the ovaries.
Release of a secondary oocyte from an ovarian follicle.
A pituitary hormone that supports ovarian follicle development and sperm production.
A pituitary hormone that triggers ovulation and stimulates gonadal steroid secretion.
A class of steroid hormones that regulates reproductive tissues and contributes to the uterine cycle.
A steroid hormone that helps maintain the uterine lining after ovulation and during pregnancy.
Attachment and embedding of an early embryo in the uterine lining.
A temporary organ enabling exchange and endocrine communication while normally keeping maternal and fetal circulations separate.
Fertilization of oocytes outside the body followed by transfer of an embryo to the uterus.
Transfer of pollen from an anther to a receptive stigma in flowering plants.
A tubular outgrowth of a pollen grain that delivers sperm cells to an ovule.
Angiosperm process in which one sperm forms a zygote and another forms triploid endosperm.
Movement of seeds away from the parent plant by wind, water, animals, or mechanical means.

sourceTitle: OpenStax Biology 2e, 12 Mendel’s Experiments and Heredity

terms.definition: The physical position of a gene or genetic marker on a chromosome.
One of two or more alternative DNA sequences at the same genetic locus.
The allele combination of an organism at one or more specified loci.
An observable or measurable characteristic produced by genotype, environment, and their interaction.
Having identical alleles at a specified locus in a diploid organism.
Having two different alleles at a specified locus in a diploid organism.
An allele expressed in the phenotype of a heterozygote under complete dominance.
An allele whose effect under complete dominance is masked in a heterozygote.
An inheritance pattern in which both alleles are distinctly expressed in a heterozygote.
An inheritance pattern in which the heterozygote has a phenotype intermediate between the two homozygotes.
The existence of more than two alternative alleles at one locus within a population.
A gene located on a sex chromosome, producing inheritance patterns that depend on chromosomal sex.
A chromosome not classified as a sex chromosome.
A heterozygous individual who can transmit a recessive disease allele without showing the disease phenotype.
A grid used to display possible gamete combinations and predict offspring genotype probabilities.
A cross with a homozygous recessive individual used to infer an unknown dominant phenotype’s genotype.
A genetic cross that tracks inheritance at one locus.
A genetic cross that tracks inheritance at two loci simultaneously.
The tendency of loci on the same chromosome to be inherited together.
The percentage of recombinant offspring, used to estimate distance between linked loci.
Maintenance of internal variables within tolerable limits despite internal or external change.
A physiological quantity monitored and regulated by a homeostatic system.
The target value or range around which a regulated variable is maintained.
Control in which a deviation triggers responses that oppose the original change.
Control in which a change triggers responses that amplify that change until an external endpoint stops the loop.
A component that detects a change in a regulated internal or external condition.
A control component that compares sensory information with a target and coordinates a response.
A tissue or organ that carries out a response directed by a control system.
A sensory receptor that responds to temperature change.
Widening of blood vessels caused by relaxation of smooth muscle in their walls.
Narrowing of blood vessels caused by contraction of smooth muscle in their walls.
Rapid involuntary skeletal-muscle contractions that increase metabolic heat production.
A disorder caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, producing severe insulin deficiency.
A disorder characterized by insulin resistance with progressive inability to maintain normal blood glucose.
An internally generated biological cycle of about 24 hours that can be synchronized by environmental cues.
Non-random differential survival and reproduction caused by heritable variation among individuals.
Differences in characteristics among individuals of the same population or species.
Differences among individuals that can be transmitted genetically to offspring.
An environmental factor that causes differences in survival or reproductive success among phenotypes.
An individual’s relative contribution of viable, fertile offspring to the next generation.
Unequal production of surviving offspring by individuals with different inherited characteristics.
Selection favoring phenotypes toward one end of a trait distribution.
Selection favoring intermediate phenotypes and acting against both extremes.
Selection favoring phenotypes at both extremes over intermediate forms.
Selection arising from differences in success at obtaining mates or achieving fertilization.
Human-directed breeding that changes trait frequencies by choosing which organisms reproduce.
Random change in allele frequencies, with stronger effects in small populations.
Genetic drift when a new population begins from a small, non-representative sample of a source population.
Sharp population reduction that randomly removes alleles and changes genetic variation.
Transfer of alleles between populations through movement and reproduction of individuals or gametes.
A null model in which allele and genotype frequencies remain constant without evolutionary forces.
The inherited ability of bacteria to survive or reproduce at an antibiotic concentration that inhibits susceptible cells.
Capacity to maintain ecological and human systems over time without exhausting their supporting resources.
Development that meets present needs while preserving future generations’ ability to meet their own needs.
Biologically productive area needed to supply a population’s resource use and absorb specified wastes.
An ecosystem’s capacity to generate renewable biological resources and absorb specified wastes.
A resource replenished naturally on a timescale compatible with its rate of use.
A resource used far faster than natural processes replace it on a human timescale.
The largest harvest rate that can be maintained without long-term depletion under stated conditions.
A benefit that people obtain from functioning ecosystems.
A material product supplied by ecosystems, such as food, fresh water, fiber, or medicine.
A benefit from ecosystem regulation of processes such as climate, floods, pollination, or disease.
A non-material ecosystem benefit involving recreation, identity, education, aesthetics, or spiritual value.
A foundational ecosystem process, such as soil formation or nutrient cycling, that enables other services.
An ecosystem’s capacity to absorb disturbance and retain its core structure and functions.
A threshold beyond which a small additional change can shift an ecosystem into a different persistent state.
A structured prediction and evaluation of likely environmental effects before a proposed action is approved.
A production model designed to minimize waste by keeping materials in use through reuse, repair, and recycling.
Short-term atmospheric conditions at a particular place and time.
The statistical pattern of weather over a long period, usually decades or longer.
Warming caused when atmospheric gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation from Earth’s surface and atmosphere.
An atmospheric gas that absorbs and emits infrared radiation at wavelengths relevant to Earth’s energy balance.
Additional warming caused by human-driven increases in atmospheric greenhouse-gas concentrations.
Long-term increase in global mean surface temperature relative to a stated reference period.
A persistent change in the statistical state of climate over decades or longer.
A change in Earth’s energy balance caused by a driver such as greenhouse gases, aerosols, or solar variation.
The fraction of incoming radiation reflected by a surface or system.
A reservoir or process that removes more carbon from the atmosphere than it releases.
A reservoir or process that releases more carbon to the atmosphere than it removes.
Capture and long-term storage of carbon in biological, geological, or engineered reservoirs.
Decline in ocean pH caused mainly by uptake of human-emitted carbon dioxide.
Increase in average sea level caused chiefly by ocean warming and loss of land ice.
Action that reduces greenhouse-gas emissions or increases removal of those gases from the atmosphere.
Adjustment to actual or expected climate effects to reduce harm or use beneficial opportunities.
A process that amplifies or dampens a climate response after an initial forcing.
Ground that remains at or below 0 °C for at least two consecutive years.
A climate-associated change in the seasonal timing of biological events such as flowering or migration.
Loss of algal symbionts or their pigments from corals under stress, leaving tissue pale and energy-limited.
